claim: Methylation of cytosines (5meC) is a widespread heritable DNA modification.
source: Methylation of cytosines (5meC) is a widespread heritable DNA modification.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DNA methylation.

claim: During mammalian development, two global demethylation events are followed by waves of de novo DNA methylation.
source: During mammalian development, two global demethylation events are followed by waves of de novo DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mammalian development.

claim: DNMT3B and H3K4 methylation are mutually exclusive in yeast expressing DNMT3B.
source: Our data demonstrate that DNMT3B and H3K4 methylation are mutually exclusive and that DNMT3B is co-localized with H3K36 methylated regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from yeast expressing DNMT3B, including ChIP-seq and DNA methylation analysis.

claim: DNMT3B is co-localized with H3K36 methylated regions in yeast.
source: Our data demonstrate that DNMT3B and H3K4 methylation are mutually exclusive and that DNMT3B is co-localized with H3K36 methylated regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ChIP-seq data showing co-localization of DNMT3B with H3K36me3.

claim: DNA methylation analysis in yeast strains without Set1 shows an increase of relative 5meC levels at the transcription start site.
source: In support of this observation, DNA methylation analysis in yeast strains without Set1 and Set2 shows an increase of relative 5meC levels at the transcription start site and a decrease in the gene-body, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data from set1Δ yeast strains.

claim: DNA methylation analysis in yeast strains without Set2 shows a decrease of relative 5meC levels in the gene-body.
source: In support of this observation, DNA methylation analysis in yeast strains without Set1 and Set2 shows an increase of relative 5meC levels at the transcription start site and a decrease in the gene-body, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data from set2Δ yeast strains.

claim: In murine male germline, H3K4me3 is strongly anti-correlated with accelerated DNA methylation.
source: We extend our observation to the murine male germline, where H3K4me3 is strongly anti-correlated while H3K36me3 correlates with accelerated DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells at different developmental stages.

claim: In murine male germline, H3K36me3 correlates with accelerated DNA methylation.
source: We extend our observation to the murine male germline, where H3K4me3 is strongly anti-correlated while H3K36me3 correlates with accelerated DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells at different developmental stages.

claim: H3K36 methylation is important for gene-body DNA methylation in vivo.
source: These results show the importance of H3K36 methylation for gene-body DNA methylation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from both yeast and mouse showing correlation between H3K36me3 and gene-body DNA methylation.

claim: In mammals, DNA methylation plays a fundamental role in processes such as imprinting, X-chromosome inactivation, transposon inactivation, and gene expression regulation.
source: In mammals, DNA methylation plays a fundamental role in processes such as imprinting, X-chromosome inactivation, transposon inactivation, and gene expression regulation (Smith and Meissner, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dysregulation of DNA methylation is a common feature in cancer.
source: Dysregulation of DNA methylation is a common feature in cancer (Eden et al., 2003; You and Jones, 2012) and a variety of human diseases are caused by defective imprinting (Peters, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A variety of human diseases are caused by defective imprinting.
source: Dysregulation of DNA methylation is a common feature in cancer (Eden et al., 2003; You and Jones, 2012) and a variety of human diseases are caused by defective imprinting (Peters, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Methylation is mainly found at symmetric CpG dinucleotides.
source: Methylation is mainly found at symmetric CpG dinucleotides, where it is introduced by the de novo DNA methyltransferases (DNMT3a and DNMT3b) and can be copied faithfully during DNA replication by the activity of a 'maintenance' DNA methyltransferase, DNMT1 (Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: De novo DNA methyltransferases DNMT3a and DNMT3b introduce methylation at CpG dinucleotides.
source: Methylation is mainly found at symmetric CpG dinucleotides, where it is introduced by the de novo DNA methyltransferases (DNMT3a and DNMT3b) and can be copied faithfully during DNA replication by the activity of a 'maintenance' DNA methyltransferase, DNMT1 (Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DNMT1 is a maintenance DNA methyltransferase that can copy methylation faithfully during DNA replication.
source: Methylation is mainly found at symmetric CpG dinucleotides, where it is introduced by the de novo DNA methyltransferases (DNMT3a and DNMT3b) and can be copied faithfully during DNA replication by the activity of a 'maintenance' DNA methyltransferase, DNMT1 (Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: 5meC can be lost by a passive mechanism, such as the failure to maintain DNA methylation through cell division.
source: In fact, 5meC can either be lost by a passive mechanism, such as the failure to maintain DNA methylation through cell division or by an active mechanism such as the removal of methylcytosine, typically via an oxidized intermediate (Pastor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: 5meC can be lost by an active mechanism such as the removal of methylcytosine, typically via an oxidized intermediate.
source: In fact, 5meC can either be lost by a passive mechanism, such as the failure to maintain DNA methylation through cell division or by an active mechanism such as the removal of methylcytosine, typically via an oxidized intermediate (Pastor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Most DNA methylation is progressively lost between fertilization and the formation of the blastula.
source: For example, most DNA methylation is progressively lost between fertilization and the formation of the blastula and global de novo DNA methylation then occurs coincidently with implantation of the embryo.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about mammalian development.

claim: Global de novo DNA methylation occurs coincidently with implantation of the embryo.
source: For example, most DNA methylation is progressively lost between fertilization and the formation of the blastula and global de novo DNA methylation then occurs coincidently with implantation of the embryo.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about mammalian development.

claim: After specification of the germ cells, most DNA methylation is lost during early primordial germ cell (PGCs) development.
source: After specification of the germ cells, most DNA methylation is lost during early primordial germ cell (PGCs) development.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about germline development.

claim: Imprints are erased during early primordial germ cell development.
source: Unlike in early embryogenesis, imprints are erased during this period.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about germline development.

claim: Genome-wide de novo methylation occurs before birth in the male germline.
source: Genome-wide de novo methylation then occurs before birth in the male germline and upon oocyte maturation in females (Smallwood et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Genome-wide de novo methylation occurs upon oocyte maturation in females.
source: Genome-wide de novo methylation then occurs before birth in the male germline and upon oocyte maturation in females (Smallwood et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DNMT3 proteins do not have strong sequence preferences beyond CpG dinucleotides.
source: DNMT3 proteins do not have strong sequence preferences beyond CpG dinucleotides (Dodge et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Active de novo DNA methyltransferases possess three different domains: the catalytic domain, an ADD domain and a PWWP domain.
source: Active de novo DNA methyltransferases possess three different domains: the catalytic domain, found at the C-terminus of the protein, an ADD domain and a PWWP domain (Figure 1A) (Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and Figure 1A showing the domain structure.

claim: The catalytic domain of active de novo DNA methyltransferases is found at the C-terminus of the protein.
source: Active de novo DNA methyltransferases possess three different domains: the catalytic domain, found at the C-terminus of the protein, an ADD domain and a PWWP domain (Figure 1A) (Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and Figure 1A showing the domain structure.

claim: DNMT3L possesses only a functional ADD domain.
source: In contrast, the inactive DNMT3L possesses only a functional ADD domain.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about DNMT3L structure.

claim: The ADD domains of all three DNMTs have been shown to preferentially bind histone 3 tails that lack methylation at lysine 4 (H3K4me0).
source: The ADD domains of all three DNMTs have been shown to preferentially bind histone 3 tails that lack methylation at lysine 4 (H3K4me0) (Ooi et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010), and this binding has been recently shown to relieve DNMT3a auto-inhibition (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ADD domain binding to H3K4me0 has been shown to relieve DNMT3a auto-inhibition.
source: The ADD domains of all three DNMTs have been shown to preferentially bind histone 3 tails that lack methylation at lysine 4 (H3K4me0) (Ooi et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010), and this binding has been recently shown to relieve DNMT3a auto-inhibition (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Genomic regions bearing H3K4 methylation are generally depleted of 5meC.
source: This is consistent with the observation that genomic regions bearing H3K4 methylation are generally depleted of 5meC (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The PWWP domain of several proteins has been shown to bind H3K36 methylation.
source: The PWWP domain of several proteins has been shown to bind H3K36 methylation (Vermeulen et al., 2010), and indeed the DNMT3a-PWWP domain has also been shown to interact with the tri-methylated lysine 36 of histone H3 (H3K36me3) in vitro (Dhayalan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The DNMT3a-PWWP domain has been shown to interact with H3K36me3 in vitro.
source: The PWWP domain of several proteins has been shown to bind H3K36 methylation (Vermeulen et al., 2010), and indeed the DNMT3a-PWWP domain has also been shown to interact with the tri-methylated lysine 36 of histone H3 (H3K36me3) in vitro (Dhayalan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The PWWP domain of DNMT3b is important in specifying the localization of DNMT3b in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Recently, it has been reported that the PWWP domain is important in specifying the localization of DNMT3b in mouse embryonic stem cells (Baubec et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Ectopically expressed murine DNMT3b methylates yeast genomic DNA.
source: S. cerevisiae does not have any endogenous cytosine DNA methyltransferases, and its DNA is therefore unmethylated. To study the activity of a de novo methyltransferase in this organism, we introduced the murine DNMT3b under the control of the inducible GAL1 promoter (Figure 1B). We measured the levels of 5-methylcytosine (5meC) in these strains using whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) (Supplementary file 1A). We observed significant levels of 5meC of DNA extracted from the exponentially growing and stationary phases of the same strain culture (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 2A), with higher methylation levels observed in stationary phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data showing 5meC in yeast expressing DNMT3b.

claim: S. cerevisiae does not have any endogenous cytosine DNA methyltransferases.
source: S. cerevisiae does not have any endogenous cytosine DNA methyltransferases, and its DNA is therefore unmethylated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: CpG dinucleotides were preferentially methylated in yeast expressing DNMT3b.
source: CpG dinucleotides were preferentially methylated, as expected from the previously characterized activity of mammalian DNMT3.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data from yeast expressing DNMT3b.

claim: The methylation levels of CpG dinucleotides range from 3.3 to 7.7% in yeast expressing DNMT3b.
source: The methylation levels of CpG dinucleotides range from 3.3 to 7.7%, depending on the yeast strain analyzed.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data.

claim: CpG methylation levels in yeast expressing DNMT3b are about 10–20 times higher than the average of other dinucleotides levels.
source: These levels are about 10–20 times higher than the average of other dinucleotides levels (Supplementary file 2A), and well above the bisulfite non-conversion rate of 0.27%, as estimated from an unmethylated lambda DNA spike-in.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data.

claim: The bisulfite non-conversion rate is 0.27%, as estimated from an unmethylated lambda DNA spike-in.
source: These levels are about 10–20 times higher than the average of other dinucleotides levels (Supplementary file 2A), and well above the bisulfite non-conversion rate of 0.27%, as estimated from an unmethylated lambda DNA spike-in.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of lambda DNA spike-in control.

claim: In yeast expressing DNMT3b, there is low methylation at the transcription start site and increasing methylation in the gene body, reaching a maximum close to the transcription termination site.
source: We also observed a striking methylation distribution within genes (Figure 1D), with low levels at the transcription start site (TSS) and increasing methylation in the gene body, reaching a maximum close to the transcription termination site (TTS).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The same pattern of DNA methylation distribution within genes is found in mammals.
source: The same pattern is found in mammals (Lister et al., 2009; Chodavarapu et al., 2010), suggesting that equivalent mechanisms regulating DNMT3 activity in mammalian genes might also be present in yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Equivalent mechanisms regulating DNMT3 activity in mammalian genes might also be present in yeast.
source: The same pattern is found in mammals (Lister et al., 2009; Chodavarapu et al., 2010), suggesting that equivalent mechanisms regulating DNMT3 activity in mammalian genes might also be present in yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of DNA methylation patterns between yeast expressing DNMT3b and mammals.

claim: In yeast, nucleosomes are well positioned at the beginning of a gene, with nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) immediately upstream of the TSS and downstream of the TTS.
source: In yeast, nucleosomes are well positioned at the beginning of a gene, with nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) immediately upstream of the TSS and downstream of the TTS (Brogaard et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Average levels of 5meC around the TSS show a periodicity of about 170 bp.
source: When average levels of 5meC are calculated around the TSS, we observed a periodicity of about 170 bp (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A similar periodicity of DNA methylation is also observed at the TTS.
source: A similar periodicity is also observed at the TTS.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data.

claim: DNMT3b preferentially methylates linker DNA compared to nucleosomal DNA.
source: From these analyses, it is evident that DNMT3b preferentially methylates non-nucleosomal DNA. We observe a 50% increase in the methylation of linker DNA compared to nucleosome bound DNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined MNase-seq and DNA methylation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a 50% increase in the methylation of linker DNA compared to nucleosome bound DNA.
source: We observe a 50% increase in the methylation of linker DNA compared to nucleosome bound DNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined MNase-seq and DNA methylation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a slight 10 bp periodicity of methylated CpG in nucleosomes.
source: We also observe a slight 10 bp periodicity of methylated CpG (Figure 2D), another feature shown in higher eukaryotes that reflects the periodicity of the DNA helix (Klug and Lutter, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to published literature.

claim: The 10 bp periodicity of methylated CpG reflects the periodicity of the DNA helix.
source: We also observe a slight 10 bp periodicity of methylated CpG (Figure 2D), another feature shown in higher eukaryotes that reflects the periodicity of the DNA helix (Klug and Lutter, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Introducing 5meC does not alter nucleosome distribution in yeast.
source: However, a comparison of DNMT3b-expressing and non-expressing strains showed no detectable change in nucleosome positioning by MNase treatment near the TSS, TTS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B and Supplementary file 3C), or elsewhere in the genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by MNase-seq data comparing DNMT3b-expressing and non-expressing strains.

claim: About 5% of yeast genes are differentially expressed between the strain expressing and non-expressing DNMT3b grown to stationary phase.
source: RNA-seq analysis identified some differentially expressed genes (about 5% of the total number of genes, with an equal number of up- and down-regulated transcripts) between the strain expressing and non-expressing DNMT3b grown to stationary phase (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1C and Supplementary file 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is an equal number of up- and down-regulated transcripts between the strain expressing and non-expressing DNMT3b.
source: RNA-seq analysis identified some differentially expressed genes (about 5% of the total number of genes, with an equal number of up- and down-regulated transcripts) between the strain expressing and non-expressing DNMT3b grown to stationary phase (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1C and Supplementary file 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The down-regulated genes in DNMT3b-expressing yeast showed enrichment for branched-chain aminoacid biosynthesis genes.
source: The down-regulated genes showed enrichment for branched-chain aminoacid biosynthesis genes, while the up-regulated ones were enriched in ribosomal biogenesis genes (Supplementary file 4B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: The up-regulated genes in DNMT3b-expressing yeast were enriched in ribosomal biogenesis genes.
source: The down-regulated genes showed enrichment for branched-chain aminoacid biosynthesis genes, while the up-regulated ones were enriched in ribosomal biogenesis genes (Supplementary file 4B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Changes in gene expression in DNMT3b-expressing yeast are likely due to stress response pathways triggered by the overexpression of MmDNMT3b, rather than by the changes in DNA methylation itself.
source: However, these changes are likely due to stress response pathways that are triggered by the overexpression of MmDNMT3b, rather than by the changes in DNA methylation itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that methylation levels do not correlate with differential expression.

claim: The levels of CpG, CpHpG, and CpHpH methylation in the up- and down-regulated genes were not significantly different.
source: In support of this view, when the levels of CpG, CpHpG, and CpHpH methylation in the up- and down-regulated genes were compared, no significant difference was evident (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The methylation levels of the differentially transcribed genes were not different from that of other members of the same Gene Ontology (GO) term.
source: Moreover, the methylation levels of the differentially transcribed genes were not different from that of other members of the same Gene Ontology (GO) term (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Yeast likely lacks proteins able to recognize and mediate 5meC effects.
source: Since DNA methylation machinery is not native in yeast, it is likely that proteins able to recognize and mediate 5meC effects are also absent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of endogenous DNA methylation machinery in yeast.

claim: DNMT3b co-localizes with methylated regions in yeast.
source: We found that, as expected, DNMT3b co-localizes with methylated regions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data for DNMT3b and DNA methylation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The distribution of DNMT3b is consistent with the distribution of DNA methylation across the gene body.
source: The distribution of DNMT3b is also consistent with the distribution of DNA methylation across the gene body (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and DNA methylation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNMT3b and 5meC are strongly anti-correlated with H3K4me3 in yeast.
source: We also observed that DNMT3b and 5meC are strongly anti-correlated with H3K4me3 and positively correlated with H3K36me3 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and DNA methylation data shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: DNMT3b and 5meC are positively correlated with H3K36me3 in yeast.
source: We also observed that DNMT3b and 5meC are strongly anti-correlated with H3K4me3 and positively correlated with H3K36me3 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and DNA methylation data shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: H3K4me3 is concentrated at the promoter in yeast.
source: By examining the distribution of histone marks across gene bodies, we found that H3K4me3 is concentrated at the promoter while H3K36me3 levels peak near the 3′ end of the gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K36me3 levels peak near the 3′ end of the gene in yeast.
source: By examining the distribution of histone marks across gene bodies, we found that H3K4me3 is concentrated at the promoter while H3K36me3 levels peak near the 3′ end of the gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ADD and PWWP domains of DNMT3B play a role in targeting the activity of the enzyme.
source: These observations suggest that the ADD and PWWP domains of DNMT3B play a role in targeting the activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between histone marks and DNA methylation.

claim: H3K4me1 shows a weak positive correlation with both 5meC levels and DNMT3b.
source: H3K4me1 shows a weak positive correlation with both 5meC levels and DNMT3b.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and DNA methylation data.

claim: 5meC and DNMT3b distribution are inversely correlated with gene transcription and Pol II abundance.
source: 5meC and DNMT3b distribution are also inversely correlated with gene transcription and Pol II abundance (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 2E–F, 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq, DNA methylation, and RNA-seq data.

claim: Both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 correlate positively with transcription in yeast.
source: Both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 correlate positively with transcription (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 levels are sufficient to predict the distribution of both DNMT3b and 5meC with very high accuracy.
source: Strikingly, we found that H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 levels are sufficient to predict the distribution of both DNMT3b and 5meC with very high accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear multivariate regression modeling shown in Figure 4C.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 are the key factors in determining the targeting of DNA methylation.
source: The prediction could only be slightly improved by using additional data, suggesting that H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 are the key factors in determining the targeting of DNA methylation (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on linear modeling results.

claim: In yeast, Set1 is responsible for the methylation of H3K4.
source: In yeast, Set1 is responsible for the methylation of H3K4, Set2 is the methyltransferase for H3K36, and Dot1 catalyzes the methylation of H3K79.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast histone methyltransferases.

claim: In yeast, Set2 is the methyltransferase for H3K36.
source: In yeast, Set1 is responsible for the methylation of H3K4, Set2 is the methyltransferase for H3K36, and Dot1 catalyzes the methylation of H3K79.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast histone methyltransferases.

claim: In yeast, Dot1 catalyzes the methylation of H3K79.
source: In yeast, Set1 is responsible for the methylation of H3K4, Set2 is the methyltransferase for H3K36, and Dot1 catalyzes the methylation of H3K79.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast histone methyltransferases.

claim: The resulting 5meC levels in set1Δ, set2Δ, and dot1Δ strains were significantly higher than background levels found in the wt strains.
source: Nonetheless, the resulting 5meC levels were still significantly higher than background levels found in the wt strains (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the set1Δ strain, regions close to the TSS contain methylation levels that are not significantly different from other regions outside of the gene.
source: In contrast, in the set1Δ strain, we found that regions close to the TSS, with high H3K4me3 and low DNA methylation in a wt strain, contain methylation levels that are not significantly different from other regions outside of the gene (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data from set1Δ strains shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: H3K4 methylation plays an active role in suppressing DNA methylation in the wt yeast.
source: This suggests that H3K4 methylation plays an active role in suppressing DNA methylation in the wt, and that this effect disappears in the set1Δ strain (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of DNA methylation patterns between wt and set1Δ strains.

claim: In a set2Δ strain, 5meC levels are reduced over gene bodies compared to wt strains.
source: In a set2Δ strain, 5meC levels are reduced over gene bodies compared to wt strains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data from set2Δ strains shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the set2Δ strain, maximum levels of DNA methylation peak outside of the gene, where H3K36me3 is not present.
source: Moreover, in this strain maximum levels of DNA methylation peak outside of the gene, where H3K36me3 is not present (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data from set2Δ strains shown in Figure 5B.

claim: H3K36me3 is responsible for recruitment of DNMT3B.
source: Thus, in this mutant strain DNA methylation is redistributed from gene bodies (H3K36me3-rich regions) to intergenic regions compared to the wt, suggesting that H3K36me3 is responsible for recruitment of DNMT3B (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the redistribution of DNA methylation in set2Δ strains.

claim: Global CpG methylation in mouse male germ cells rises from 7% at E13.5 to 55% at E16.5 and reaches at 75% by P2.5.
source: Consistent with previous observations about the timing of de novo DNA methylation in the developing mouse germline, global CpG methylation rises from 7% at E13.5 to 55% at E16.5 and reaches at 75% by P2.5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The entire male germline genome is methylated by default, except for regions of H3K4 methylation such as TSSs which antagonize de novo DNA methylation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the entire male germline genome is methylated by default, except for regions of H3K4 methylation such as TSSs which antagonize de novo DNA methylation (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There exist 'early methylating' regions that reach their final methylation state by E16.5 in mouse male germ cells.
source: However, charting the progression of DNA methylation over time, it is apparent that there exist 'early methylating' regions that reach their final methylation state by E16.5 and 'late methylating' regions that undergo substantial DNA methylation between E16.5 and P2.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells at different developmental stages.

claim: There exist 'late methylating' regions that undergo substantial DNA methylation between E16.5 and P2.5 in mouse male germ cells.
source: However, charting the progression of DNA methylation over time, it is apparent that there exist 'early methylating' regions that reach their final methylation state by E16.5 and 'late methylating' regions that undergo substantial DNA methylation between E16.5 and P2.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells at different developmental stages.

claim: Heavily transcribed regions of chromosomes showed much higher DNA methylation at E16.5 than less transcribed regions in mouse male germ cells.
source: We observed that heavily transcribed regions of chromosomes showed much higher DNA methylation at E16.5 than less transcribed regions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: While the TSS of active genes was unmethylated, gene bodies of actively transcribed genes were typically early-methylators in mouse male germ cells.
source: Furthermore, while the TSS of active genes was unmethylated, gene bodies of actively transcribed genes were typically early-methylators (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: Transcriptional initiation correlates negatively with de novo DNA methylation in mouse male germ cells.
source: Thus, transcriptional initiation correlates negatively with de novo DNA methylation while transcriptional elongation correlates positively with de novo methylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq and bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells.

claim: Transcriptional elongation correlates positively with de novo DNA methylation in mouse male germ cells.
source: Thus, transcriptional initiation correlates negatively with de novo DNA methylation while transcriptional elongation correlates positively with de novo methylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq and bisulfite sequencing data from mouse male germ cells.

claim: H3K4me3 at E13.5 correlates with low DNA methylation at all subsequent time points in mouse male germ cells.
source: H3K4me3 at E13.5 correlates with low DNA methylation at all subsequent time points (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Genes with high H3K36me3 levels at E13.5 showed significantly elevated gene-body DNA methylation at E16.5 in mouse male germ cells.
source: Genes with high H3K36me3 levels at E13.5 showed significantly elevated gene-body DNA methylation at E16.5, consistent with H3K36me3 accelerating DNA methylation (Figure 6B,C,D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6B,C,D,F.

claim: H3K36me3 accelerates DNA methylation in mouse male germ cells.
source: Genes with high H3K36me3 levels at E13.5 showed significantly elevated gene-body DNA methylation at E16.5, consistent with H3K36me3 accelerating DNA methylation (Figure 6B,C,D,F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between H3K36me3 and early DNA methylation.

claim: H3K36me3 appears to direct DNA methylation in mammalian cells.
source: Thus, H3K36me3 appears to direct DNA methylation in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between H3K36me3 and DNA methylation in mouse male germ cells.

claim: The activity of DNMT3B is guided by the interactions of the ADD and PWWP domains with histone tails.
source: This suggests that the activity of DNMT3B is guided by the interactions of the ADD and PWWP domains with histone tails.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between histone marks and DNA methylation patterns.

claim: In embryonic stem cells, the PWWP domain is responsible for the targeting of DNMT3b to regions enriched for the H3K36me3.
source: It has been recently shown (Baubec et al., 2015) that in embryonic stem cells the PWWP domain is responsible for the targeting of DNMT3b to regions enriched for the H3K36me3.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The reintroduction of DNMT3b into methylation deficient DNMT1/DNMT3A/DNMT3B triple KO (TKO) ES cells partially restores 5meC levels.
source: Similarly to our finding in yeast, the reintroduction of DNMT3b into methylation deficient DNMT1/DNMT3A/DNMT3B triple KO (TKO) ES cells partially restores 5meC levels.
evidence: This claim is based on published literature.

claim: Methylation levels are higher at H3K36me3 sites in ES cells, a trend eliminated by the ablation of the H3K36me3 methyltransferase Setd2.
source: Methylation levels are higher at H3K36me3 sites, a trend eliminated by the ablation of the H3K36me3 methyltransferase Setd2 (Baubec et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In yeast expressing DNMT3b, there is an anti-correlation between transcript levels and DNA methylation.
source: In our yeast system, we detected an anti-correlation between transcript levels and DNA methylation, while we found a positive correlation in germ cells as was shown in ES cells (Baubec et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and DNA methylation data from yeast.

claim: In germ cells, there is a positive correlation between transcript levels and DNA methylation.
source: In our yeast system, we detected an anti-correlation between transcript levels and DNA methylation, while we found a positive correlation in germ cells as was shown in ES cells (Baubec et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and DNA methylation data from mouse germ cells and a citation to published literature.

claim: The discrepancy between the findings in yeast and germ cells can be explained by the difference in the length of their genes.
source: The discrepancy between the findings in yeast and germ cells can be explained by the difference in the length of their genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of gene structures between yeast and mammals.

claim: Yeast genes are relatively small compared to genes in higher eukaryotes so H3K4 methylation can spread within the body of the gene.
source: Yeast genes are relatively small compared to genes in higher eukaryotes so, H3K4 methylation can spread within the body of the gene, thus preventing the binding of the DNMT3-ADD domain to the N-terminus of histone H3 and reducing its activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of H3K4me3 distribution in yeast genes.

claim: In mammals, H3K4me is localized to the start of the gene, and does not spread significantly within the gene body.
source: In contrast, in mammals, H3K4me is localized to the start of the gene, and does not spread significantly within the gene body.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about histone mark distribution in mammals.

claim: In mature oocytes, actively transcribed gene bodies have far higher levels of DNA methylation than less transcribed genes and intergenic regions.
source: In mature oocytes, which have intermediate global levels of CpG methylation (∼50%), similar to male E16.5 PGCs, actively transcribed gene bodies have far higher levels of DNA methylation than less transcribed genes and intergenic regions (Smallwood et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In oocytes, intragenic CpG islands show far higher DNA methylation than other CpG islands.
source: Also, in oocytes, intragenic CpG islands show far higher DNA methylation than other CpG islands (Smallwood et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Transcriptional read-through is a common feature of maternally imprinted loci.
source: Transcriptional read-through is a common feature of maternally imprinted loci (Weaver and Bartolomei, 2014) and ablation of an upstream promoter prevents proper methylation of the imprinted Gnas locus (Chotalia et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ablation of an upstream promoter prevents proper methylation of the imprinted Gnas locus.
source: Transcriptional read-through is a common feature of maternally imprinted loci (Weaver and Bartolomei, 2014) and ablation of an upstream promoter prevents proper methylation of the imprinted Gnas locus (Chotalia et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In mammalian soma, inactive X-chromosome shows higher promoter methylation but markedly lower intragenic methylation.
source: In mammalian soma, inactive X-chromosome shows higher promoter methylation, consistent with its silent state, but markedly lower intragenic methylation (Hellman and Chess, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Transcriptional elongation is correlated with DNA methylation in tumor cells.
source: Transcriptional elongation is also correlated with DNA methylation in tumor cells (Jin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Direct recruitment of DNMTs by H3K36me3 is the most likely mechanism for the correlation between transcriptional read-through and DNA methylation.
source: It has been suggested that transcriptional read-through could 'open' chromatin for DNMTs, or that heterochromatin is physically inaccessible to DNMTs. We suggest however that direct recruitment of DNMTs by H3K36me3 is the most likely mechanism for the correlation between transcriptional read-through and DNA methylation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: H3K36me3 functions both to suppress intragenic transcriptional initiation through recruitment of histone deacetylases, and to promote DNA methylation.
source: H3K36me3 functions both to suppress intragenic transcriptional initiation through recruitment of histone deacetylases, and to promote DNA methylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and established knowledge about H3K36me3 function.

claim: H3K36me3 and DNA methylation likely cooperate to induce lasting silencing of transcriptional initiation at target loci.
source: These marks likely cooperate to induce lasting silencing of transcriptional initiation at target loci (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculation based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: H3K36me3 and DNA methylation could cooperate to silence transposons in the germline and other periods of de novo methylation.
source: Intragenic TSSs originating at transposons have the potential to generate truncated or transposon/gene hybrid transcripts that could be deleterious to cell survival. H3K36me3 and DNA methylation could cooperate to silence these transposons in the germline and other periods of de novo methylation, and to maintain silencing through development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: H3K36me3-mediated DNA methylation may serve to ensure the dominance of one promoter in a given cell type where multiple TSSs exist for a gene.
source: Moreover, where multiple TSSs exist for a gene, as in many imprinted loci, H3K36me3-mediated DNA methylation may serve to ensure the dominance of one promoter in a given cell type.
evidence: This is speculation based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: Only one H3K36 methyltransferase, SETD2, can catalyze the conversion of H3K36me2 to me3 in mammals.
source: A number of H3K36 methyltransferases exist in mammals but only one, SETD2, can catalyze the conversion of H3K36me2 to me3 (Wagner and Carpenter, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Setd2−/− mice exhibit profound vascular defects and die at E10.5–E11.5.
source: Setd2−/− mice exhibit profound vascular defects and die at E10.5–E11.5 (Hu et al., 2010), while Setd2−/− are defective for differentiation toward endoderm (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Setd2−/− cells are defective for differentiation toward endoderm.
source: Setd2−/− mice exhibit profound vascular defects and die at E10.5–E11.5 (Hu et al., 2010), while Setd2−/− are defective for differentiation toward endoderm (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Setd2 is a tumor suppressor mutated frequently in leukemia.
source: Setd2 is also a tumor suppressor mutated frequently in leukemia (Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: All catalytically active DNMT3-family methyltransferases in animals contain PWWP domains.
source: All catalytically active DNMT3-family methyltransferases in animals contain PWWP domains, and accordingly, gene body DNA methylation is observed in all animals that have retained DNMT3 enzymes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about DNMT3 structure across animals.

claim: Gene body DNA methylation is observed in all animals that have retained DNMT3 enzymes.
source: All catalytically active DNMT3-family methyltransferases in animals contain PWWP domains, and accordingly, gene body DNA methylation is observed in all animals that have retained DNMT3 enzymes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about DNA methylation patterns across animals.

claim: Preferential methylation of gene bodies over intergenic regions is observed for invertebrates such as honey bees, sea squirts, and sea anemones.
source: Preferential methylation of gene bodies over intergenic regions is observed for invertebrates such as honey bees (Apis mellifera), sea squirts (Ciona intestinalis), sea anemones (Nematostella vectensis) (Zemach and Grafi, 2003; Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is a strong correlation between gene-body H3K36me3 in Drosophila melanogaster genes and DNA methylation of homologous gene bodies in other invertebrates.
source: While the relationship between relative gene expression and gene-body methylation varies across these species, there is a strong correlation between gene-body H3K36me3 in Drosophila melanogaster genes and DNA methylation of homologous gene bodies in other invertebrates (Nanty et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DNA methylation is associated with gene bodies in zebrafish.
source: DNA methylation is also associated with gene bodies in zebrafish (Danio rerio) (Zemach and Grafi, 2003) and in mammalian contexts as discussed above.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Some chlorophyte algae have a 'chlorophyte-type cytosine methylase' which is fused to two PWWP domains.
source: Finally, some chlorophyte algae have a 'chlorophyte-type cytosine methylase', which evolved independently of DNMT3-family methyltransferases, which is fused to two PWWP domains (Iyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: H3K36me3 could be relevant to DNA methylation targeting throughout the plant and animal kingdoms.
source: Thus, H3K36me3 could be relevant to DNA methylation targeting throughout the plant and animal kingdoms.
evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation of PWWP domains and H3K36me3 across species.
